verdict.summary: Mercury has no self-serve OAuth console. You must submit Mercury's OAuth Request Form and wait for Mercury to issue a client ID and secret, and Mercury publishes no approval timeline. Your own account can be connected in minutes with a Mercury API token instead of OAuth.
verdict.hands_on_effort: About 2-4 hours of active work spread over the request, setup details and Composio configuration; the approval wait is not published
verdict.time_to_first_connection: Minutes for your own account using a Mercury API token; OAuth depends on Mercury approval
verdict.approval_wait: Unknown. Mercury publishes no numeric timeline and says it may ask for more information (f5).

gates.name: Own account via API token (no OAuth app)
gates.unlocks: Calls to Mercury's API against your own company account, using a Mercury API token created in the Mercury dashboard. This does not use OAuth and does not give customers a connect flow.
limits: Read Only tokens need no IP allowlist; Read and Write tokens require an IP allowlist, and Mercury offers no way around that requirement.
Tokens not used within any 45-day period are automatically deleted; admins get an email seven days before.
Creating a token requires a user with sufficient permissions; an admin must grant the option if it is missing.

gates.name: Partner-approved OAuth client with sandbox test credentials
gates.unlocks: OAuth authorization code flow with PKCE against Mercury's sandbox using the test-client credentials Mercury issues, so you can test the connect flow end to end.
limits: Access requires prior approval through Mercury's OAuth Request Form; it is scoped to companies building integrations for Mercury customers.
Redirect URIs must match the URLs registered with your client.
Refresh-token lifetime and access-token expiry are not stated in the pages reviewed.
Whether the client is limited to read-only access is a third-party claim only.
gates.time_to_reach: Unknown. Mercury publishes no approval timeline; it weighs security, use case fit and regulatory considerations.

gates.name: Production OAuth for Mercury customers
gates.unlocks: Production OAuth client credentials that let your customers connect their Mercury accounts through your Composio-based agent.
limits: No numeric rate limits are published; third-party reports say per-endpoint thresholds are not prominently published.
Confirm with Mercury before public use that no further review applies.
gates.time_to_reach: Unknown. No marketplace listing, security assessment or install-cap review was found beyond the partner approval form; this is an inference from the pages reviewed.

steps.title: Decide which path you need
steps.detail: If you only need your own Mercury account, use an API token (Gate 1) and skip OAuth. Mercury's OAuth2 flow is for companies building integrations for Mercury customers, so continue with the steps below only if your agent will serve other Mercury customers.
gotchas: A developer connecting only their own account is pointed to the Getting Started flow, not OAuth.

steps.title: Submit the Mercury OAuth Request Form
steps.detail: Open the publicly reachable 'Mercury OAuth Request Form' Notion page and fill in company name and website, company address, a short company description, details of the product you plan to integrate, and how the API will be used. Mercury may ask for more information.
gotchas: There is no self-serve developer console for OAuth; the request form is the only route to a client.
Mercury weighs security, use case fit and regulatory considerations, so describe your use case concretely.

steps.title: Draft the setup materials
steps.detail: Draft the text for the terms of service and privacy policy pages, a short company description and the product description for your integration. You publish the pages and supply a logo, since Mercury asks for links to terms, privacy policy and logo.
gotchas: The pages must be live at public URLs before you submit the setup details.

steps.title: Prepare a GPG public key
steps.detail: Create a GPG key pair and keep the private key. Export the public key so Mercury can encrypt client credentials to you.
gotchas: Mercury sends the client ID and secret using this key, so losing the private key may block you from reading them.

steps.title: Send the post-approval setup details
steps.detail: After Mercury approves the request, reply with your production redirect URI, any optional dev/test redirect URIs, links to terms, privacy policy and logo, and your GPG public key. Set the production redirect URI to the Composio callback URL shown in your Composio auth config.

values.label: Redirect URI
values.value: Composio callback URL (see the Composio callout on this page)

gotchas: Redirect URIs must exactly match what is registered; Mercury's authorize endpoint rejects unknown clients.
Mercury has not confirmed it will accept Composio's callback URL. Ask during this exchange.

steps.title: Receive client credentials
steps.detail: Mercury sends your client ID and client secret, plus separate test-client credentials for its sandbox. Decrypt the message with your GPG private key.

steps.title: Enter the credentials in Composio
steps.detail: In Composio, create a custom auth config for Mercury. Enter the client ID and client secret from Mercury, and set the scope to the values below. Use the test-client credentials first.

values.label: Redirect URI
values.value: Composio callback URL (see the Composio callout on this page)

gotchas: The official docs do not list scope names; confirm 'read' and 'offline_access' with Mercury before relying on them.

steps.title: Verify the authorization and token endpoints
steps.detail: Check that the authorize request at oauth2.mercury.com/oauth2/auth includes client_id, redirect_uri, a space-separated scope, response_type=code, a state of 8+ characters, and PKCE code_challenge with method S256. Then confirm the token endpoint exchanges the code for an access token.

steps.title: Test the connect flow in the sandbox
steps.detail: Run a full connect with the sandbox test client: authorize, receive the code, exchange it for tokens, make a read call and record the token expiry. Use the Mercury sandbox for any API calls that change state.
gotchas: Refresh-token lifetime is not documented in the pages reviewed; measure it during testing.

steps.title: Confirm the production path with Mercury
steps.detail: Before opening the integration to customers, ask Mercury in writing whether any review, security assessment or listing applies beyond the approval form. Also ask for the production scopes, token lifetimes and rate limits.
gotchas: No install caps or public rate-limit thresholds were found.

steps.title: Confirm write access
steps.detail: Ask Mercury whether an OAuth partner client can perform writes such as payments. Third-party reports say the OAuth scope set is read-only, and payments are described under API token scopes instead.
gotchas: Do not design payment features around OAuth until Mercury confirms it.

steps.title: Consider the dynamic-registration MCP alternative
steps.detail: Mercury's hosted MCP server supports Dynamic Client Registration, so an MCP client can register its own credentials without partner approval. It is read-only per third-party reports and client names must not contain 'Mercury'. Use it only if read access meets your need.
gotchas: Client names containing 'Mercury' are reported to be rejected.
The MCP authorize and token endpoints were not checked in this research.

requirements.detail: Required before any OAuth client exists. Submit company name and website, company address, company description, product details and API use.
The OAuth2 flow is for companies building integrations for Mercury customers. Own-account-only use goes through API tokens.

requirements.item: Terms of service, privacy policy and logo links
requirements.detail: Required in the post-approval setup details.
Used by Mercury to deliver client credentials securely.
Must match a registered URL. Production URI plus optional dev/test URIs.
Mercury supports the authorization code grant and PKCE; use S256 for the code challenge.

requirements.item: API token write scopes need an IP allowlist
requirements.detail: Read and Write API tokens require an IP allowlist; Mercury offers no way around it. Read Only tokens do not.
The user creating an API token must have the permission; an admin grants it if missing.

scopes.effect: Named only by a third-party analysis. The official OAuth reference does not list scope names, so confirm with Mercury before requesting it.
Named only by a third-party analysis; suggests refresh tokens are supported. Refresh-token lifetime is unconfirmed.
Payment action under a Custom API token, approval-gated. It is not a documented OAuth scope, so it does not apply to the OAuth client.

blockers.symptom: The OAuth2 page says the flow is for companies building integrations for Mercury customers; you are told to use the Getting Started flow.
blockers.cause: Mercury scopes the OAuth flow to integrations for customers, not to a developer's own account.
blockers.fix: Use a Mercury API token for your own account (Gate 1), or submit the OAuth Request Form if you serve other customers.

blockers.symptom: No developer console shows an OAuth client, and the docs say access requires prior approval.
blockers.cause: Mercury has no self-serve OAuth console; clients are issued after the partner approval form and a manual exchange.
blockers.fix: Submit the Mercury OAuth Request Form and wait for Mercury to send client credentials.

blockers.symptom: The authorize endpoint rejects your client_id with invalid_client, 'The requested OAuth 2.0 Client does not exist.'
blockers.cause: No OAuth client is registered for that ID; a registered client is needed before the flow works.
blockers.fix: Confirm you have the client ID Mercury issued and that it is entered correctly in the Composio auth config.

blockers.symptom: Mercury rejects the callback URL or the authorization fails with a redirect mismatch.
blockers.cause: redirect_uri must match a URL registered with the client, and Mercury has not confirmed it accepts Composio's callback URL.
blockers.fix: Register the exact Composio callback URL in the setup details; if Mercury refuses it, ask which callback it will accept.

blockers.symptom: Write or payment calls fail when using the OAuth client.
blockers.cause: Third-party reports say OAuth access is read-only; payments are documented under API token scopes, and write API tokens require an IP allowlist.
blockers.fix: Confirm write capability with Mercury. For payments, use a Custom API token with the needed scope and an IP allowlist.

blockers.symptom: An MCP dynamic-registration client is rejected.
blockers.cause: A community note says client names must not contain the word 'Mercury'.
blockers.fix: Rename the client to a name without 'Mercury'.

blockers.symptom: API token stops working after a period without use.
blockers.cause: Tokens unused for 45 days are automatically deleted, and over-broad tokens are downgraded after 45 days of under-use.
blockers.fix: Keep the token in use or recreate it; admins receive an email seven days before the action.

blockers.cause: Mercury has rate limits, but per-endpoint thresholds are not published.
blockers.fix: Back off and retry; ask Mercury for the limits that apply to your client.

composio.note: No Composio-managed OAuth app is indicated for Mercury. Plan on registering your own Mercury OAuth client after Mercury's partner approval, then entering its client ID and secret in Composio as a custom auth config. Mercury's partner OAuth is not self-serve. Whether Mercury will accept Composio's callback URL as a registered redirect URI is unverified; confirm during approval. Scopes 'read' and 'offline_access' come from a third-party analysis only.

evidence.claim: Access to Mercury's OAuth API requires prior approval, obtained by submitting Mercury's request form first.
evidence.quote: OAuth access to Mercury’s API requires prior approval.

evidence.claim: The approval request asks for company name and website, company address, a short company description, product details and how the API will be used.
evidence.quote: Details about the product you plan to integrate with Mercury

evidence.claim: The approval request form is a publicly reachable Notion page titled 'Mercury OAuth Request Form'.
evidence.quote: Mercury OAuth Request Form | Notion

evidence.claim: Approval timelines vary with integration complexity; Mercury may ask for more information; no numeric timeline is published.
evidence.quote: Approval timelines vary depending on integration complexity

evidence.claim: After approval, Mercury asks for production redirect URI, optional dev/test URIs, terms, privacy policy and logo links, and a GPG public key for delivering client credentials.
evidence.quote: Your GPG public key so we can securely send client credentials

evidence.claim: Mercury delivers the client ID and secret plus separate test-client credentials for its sandbox.
evidence.quote: we will securely share your client ID and client secret as well as credentials for a test client

evidence.claim: Mercury's OAuth2 implementation supports the authorization code grant and PKCE.
evidence.quote: supports the Authorization Code Grant Type and Authorization Code Flow with Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE)

evidence.claim: The authorize endpoint is oauth2.mercury.com/oauth2/auth and takes client_id, redirect_uri (must match a registered URL), required space-separated scope, response_type=code, optional state (8+ characters), and optional PKCE parameters (S256).
evidence.quote: Must match one of the URLs registered with the client.

evidence.claim: The OAuth2 API reference includes a token endpoint that exchanges an authorization code for an access token.
evidence.quote: Exchange an authorization code for an access token

evidence.claim: The authorize endpoint is live and answers an unknown client_id with invalid_client, so a registered client is required.
evidence.quote: The requested OAuth 2.0 Client does not exist.

evidence.claim: Mercury's official OAuth reference does not list scope names; scope is a space-separated list of requested scopes.
evidence.quote: A space-separated list of scopes that your client requests.

evidence.claim: A third-party analysis reports Mercury documents only two OAuth scopes, read and offline_access, and no documented OAuth scope moves money.
evidence.quote: Mercury documents only two OAuth scopes, read and offline_access

evidence.claim: Mercury API tokens come in three tiers: Read Only, Read and Write (needs IP allowlist), and Custom (only granted scopes such as RequestSendMoney).
evidence.quote: Custom: Can only perform requests on the specific scopes granted.

evidence.claim: Write scopes on API tokens require an IP allowlist, with no way around it; read-only tokens do not need one.
evidence.quote: We do not offer a way to circumvent this security requirement right now.

evidence.claim: API tokens unused for 45 days are automatically deleted; over-broad tokens are downgraded after 45 days of under-use; admins get an email seven days before.
evidence.quote: Tokens that are not used within any 45 day period are automatically deleted.

evidence.claim: The pages checked describe no marketplace listing, security assessment, or install-cap review beyond the partner approval form.
Mercury's hosted MCP server supports OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration, so a client can get its own credentials without partner approval.
evidence.quote: Nobody has to create an app for you first.

evidence.claim: A third-party report says Mercury's MCP access is read-only and limited to certain account data.
evidence.quote: Access is read-only and limited to certain account data

evidence.claim: A community note says client names used in MCP dynamic registration must not contain the word 'Mercury'.
evidence.quote: Client names must not contain "Mercury."

evidence.claim: Creating an API token requires a user with sufficient permissions; an admin must grant them if the option is missing.

evidence.claim: Aggregators such as Truto advertise Mercury connectivity with no OAuth app creation on the developer's side, an alternative to a direct partner app.
evidence.quote: We handle all OAuth and API key flows — you don’t need to create the OAuth app.

evidence.claim: A third-party guide says Mercury has no self-serve developer console for OAuth; the developer submits a request and waits for credentials.
evidence.quote: Mercury does not offer a self-serve developer console for OAuth.

evidence.claim: A third-party report says Mercury has rate limits, but per-endpoint thresholds are not prominently published.

evidence.claim: Mercury runs a sandbox for testing API calls, and approved OAuth clients get sandbox test credentials.
evidence.quote: Our Sandbox environment is designed to make it easy for you to test API calls in a safe, simulated version of Mercury

open_questions: No Composio toolkit exists for Mercury, so whether Composio's callback URL can be registered with Mercury is unknown; confirm during the approval exchange.
Mercury publishes no approval timeline, no install caps, and no public rate-limit numbers.
The official docs do not name the OAuth scopes; 'read' and 'offline_access' come from a third-party analysis and need confirming with Mercury.
Refresh-token lifetime and expiry are not stated in the pages read; offline_access suggests refresh is supported, but this is unconfirmed.
Whether an OAuth partner client is limited to read-only access is only a third-party claim.
The MCP authorize and token endpoints were not probed: mcp.mercury.com was blocked as a non-public host in this environment.
Whether the approval process has a fee, minimum company stage, or domain verification is unknown.
No marketplace or security review was found, but this is inferred from the pages checked, not confirmed by Mercury.
